chunk_findings.detail: The new pre-commit path calls `RC.problem(text)` and then, unconditionally (no `continue`/`else`), calls `RC.edited(text)` on the *same* text. A staged markdown file whose region markers are broken — e.g. delete a region's end marker, or paste a second copy of a region block into `docs/roadmap.md` — is exactly the input `problem()` is written for ("a file whose markers cannot be read is named too"), so `why` is truthy and the file is already appended to `bad`; then the code still hands that same unparseable text to `edited()`. `edited()` must re-derive which regions are edited, i.e. it goes through the same parser as `RC.regions`, and that parser does not return politely on malformed input: ops.py:_region_edit wraps the identical call in `try: ... except RG.RegionError: return "broken"` (`ddflow/services/export/ops.py`, the hunk added in this same change), and no such guard exists here. `_edited_regions` is invoked from the git pre-commit path with no exception handling around it, so with the input above the hook dies with an uncaught `RegionError` traceback instead of printing the intended "staged ddflow region(s) do not match their recorded digest" verdict and exit code — the check that was supposed to catch a hand-edited region refuses to run at all on the malformed file, and in the tolerant-implementation case it at least emits a bogus "region X was edited by hand" line for a file that is broken rather than edited. Either way the `edited` call belongs behind `if why: ... continue` or inside a `try/except RG.RegionError`.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_blank` runs `_STAMPED.finditer` over the whole document and replaces every match (and, when the matching `<!-- ddflow:end NAME -->` exists, everything up to the end of that line) with spaces, with no check that the match lies outside a region body. Any line in a document that starts like adopt's stamped begin marker is therefore blanked even when it is inside a region. Take a document whose region body (rendered from a template, e.g. a doc that illustrates the pin syntax) contains

```
<!-- ddflow:begin roadmap body-sha256=<H of the true body> -->
pin syntax:
<!-- ddflow:begin notes ddflow=v1 fmt=2 sha=abc -->
notes
<!-- ddflow:end notes -->
<!-- ddflow:end roadmap -->
```

`_parsed` calls `RG.parse(_blank(text))`, so `Region.content` now holds spaces where the example was. `is_edited` then computes `F.body_digest` over that altered content, which no longer equals the `<H>` the exporter wrote, so an untouched region is reported as hand-edited: `edited()` returns `["doc/roadmap"]`, the pre-commit check refuses a valid staged doc, and doctor reports a stale region. Even a lone stamped begin line (no end marker) inside a region body corrupts that region's digest the same way. The symmetric case is a fail-open: if adopt pins content that itself contains a whole region (begin and end markers both inside the blanked block), the region's markers are erased before parsing, so `_parsed`/`edited`/`mask` never see it and a hand-edited region inside the pinned block goes unreported. Blanking only stamped blocks whose span lies outside every parsed region (or parsing first and blanking outside region spans) would fix both.

chunk_findings.detail: `report.checked["doctypes"] = count` stores a bare `int` in the same mapping that other check families populate with collections: the surrounding, unchanged code in `docscheck_run.py:143` does `docs = set(report.checked["docs"])` to build the set of checked documents passed to `restrict()`. That line can only work because `checked` values are iterables (paths/kinds), so storing an `int` here breaks the invariant of the mapping. Any consumer that treats `checked` uniformly — iterating a family's value, calling `len(v)` to render the per-family count in the digest, or wrapping it with `set()` the way the diff path already wraps `"docs"` — will raise `TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable` / `object of type 'int' has no len()` as soon as a document is validated, which happens on every run because shipped types are always loaded via `types_of()`. The intended value is the collection of validated paths (`len()` then yields the count), not the count itself.

chunk_findings.detail:
The closing-fence test `elif not line.strip().strip("`~")` is true for *any* line that is whitespace-only, not just a real fence line, because `"".strip()` is already `""`. Blank lines inside a fenced block are common, and they are yielded by `lines()` with `code=True`, so they reach this branch with `fence` set. Given

```
## S
```python
a = 1

b = 2
```
```

the first code line sets `fence="python"` and appends `"python"` to every live part; the empty line then clears `fence`; the next code line (`b = 2`) has `code=True` and `fence is None`, so it is taken as a *new* opening fence, `_FENCE_OPEN` does not match it, and `""` is appended as a code language. `Part.code_langs` therefore becomes `["python", ""]` instead of `["python"]`. With two or more blank lines a single block is reported as three or more blocks. Any rule that counts blocks (`code_blocks {lang, min}`) or flags untagged fences then sees a number that does not correspond to the document — the inflated count can satisfy a `min` for a section that really contains only one block, and spurious `""` entries can trip an "every block declares a language" style check. The same line also strips both `` ` `` and `~` regardless of the character that opened the fence, so a `~~~` line inside a ```` ``` ```` block (or a ```` ``` ```` line inside a `~~~` block) clears `fence` the same way. The close should be tested against the opening fence character and its length, and should not treat an empty line as a close.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_ROW = r"^\s*\|.*\|\s*$"` requires a leading *and* trailing pipe, while `_DELIM` deliberately makes the outer pipes optional (`^\s*\|?\s*:?-{2,}:?\s*...\|?\s*$`). A valid GFM table written without outer pipes therefore yields `Part.tables == 0`:

```
Name | Age
---- | ---
Ada  | 36
```

`_DELIM` matches the `---- | ---` line, but `_ROW.match(prev)` on `"Name | Age"` fails, so `table` is `False` in `_read` (line 146) and a `has_table: true` requirement is reported as unmet for a document that does contain a table. The gate that decides "previous line is a table row" needs to accept pipe-only-inner rows, or `_DELIM`'s optional outer pipes are dead code.

If the scoped section has no prose lines (prose deliberately excludes code blocks, comments and tables — the docstring of `no_ask_placeholder` confirms this exclusion), `rows` is empty, so for any regex that can match the empty string `rx.search("")` returns a match at offset 0, `_row_at([], 0)` returns `max(len([]) - 1, 0) == 0`, and `rows[0]` raises `IndexError`, aborting the whole check run with a traceback instead of emitting a finding. Concrete input: a type TOML containing `{ kind = "forbidden_whole_text", section = "Usage", regex = "(?i)tbd|fixme|" }` where the `Usage` section contains only a fenced code block; the join is `""`, the trailing empty alternative matches, and the function indexes an empty list. chunk_findings.detail: `prev` is initialized to `0` (line 52), which is the document-root level the markdownlint/MD001-style check is supposed to compare the first heading against, but the condition is guarded with `if prev and ...`. Because `0` is falsy, the first heading of the document is never checked: given a document whose first heading is `### Deep` (or `## Overview`) and no preceding heading, `no_skipped_levels` yields no finding at all, even though the level jumps from the root 0 to 2/3. The concrete failing input is a single `## Overview` heading at line 1 — the loop enters with `prev == 0`, the `and` short-circuits, and no finding is emitted.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_ROW` was widened from `^\s*\|.*\|\s*$` (leading *and* trailing outer pipe required) to `^.*\|.*$` (any line containing a pipe). Its sibling `_DELIM` regex is deliberately permissive and accepts a bare `---` (or `----`) as a valid one-column delimiter row: `^\s*\|?\s*:?-{2,}:?...` matches `---` with every optional group empty. Table detection is `_DELIM.match(line) and _ROW.match(prev)`, so any line containing a pipe that is immediately followed by `---` now counts as a table. Concrete input:

```
The two flags are `--a | --b`
---
```

Markdown renders this as a setext heading (or, after a list item, a thematic break), not a table, but `_DELIM.match("---")` is true and `_ROW.match("The two flags are `--a | --b`")` is now also true, so `tables` becomes 1 for that section. Before this change the same input yielded `tables == 0` because `_ROW` required outer pipes, so this is a new false positive: a section rule of the `has_table` family (e.g. a required table) is satisfied by prose that merely contains a `|` above a `---` rule, and the structural parse can no longer be trusted for those sections. The same happens with any `prev` line containing a single pipe above a one-cell delimiter such as `--- | ---`, since the parser does not compare cell counts.

chunk_findings.detail:
`re.compile(..., re.I)` makes the `match == "regex"` branch case-insensitive, whereas `re.fullmatch(heading, t)` in the previous code used the default flags and was case-sensitive. Rules are TOML data, so this loosens every existing regex heading check in any type descriptor without the type changing. Concrete case: a type with `[[sections]] heading = "^API$"`, `match = "regex"` (author intent: the section must be titled `API`) — previously a document containing `## api` failed the required-section/order check, now `_locate` returns that part and the check passes. Symmetrically, `heading = "^[A-Z][a-z]+$"` now accepts `## overview`. None of the new tests cover this (the added heading test only exercises `spec`'s load-time refusal of an invalid regex), so the semantic change is untested and undocumented; if case-insensitive regex matching is intended it should be an explicit, tested decision rather than a side effect of fixing the unreachable `except`. To preserve the old behaviour the regex branch must be compiled without `re.I`:

```python
rx = re.compile(heading if match == "regex" else re.escape(heading),
                0 if match == "regex" else re.I)
```

(The previously reported `_locate` defect — the `try/except re.error` wrapping the lambda *construction* instead of its *use* — is indeed fixed by this delta: the compile now happens inside the `try`, and a hand-built type with `heading = "Over("` reads as absent rather than raising. Confirmed findings 2, 4, 5, 6 each have a matching regression test here; finding 1 is refuted and finding 3 was superseded, so none are re-reported.)

For `lint_command = "markdownlint {path}"` the resulting string is `markdownlint docs/Release Notes.md`; whether `CommandRunner`/`Declared` splits with `shlex` (argv becomes `['markdownlint', 'docs/Release', 'Notes.md']`, so the wrong file is linted) or uses a shell (the same wrong split, plus command injection via a filename containing `` ` ``/`;`/`$()`), the lint result is wrong or silently skipped for any document whose path contains whitespace or shell metacharacters. The command template is shipped/trusted, but the substituted path is attacker-controllable by adding a suitably named file to the PR.

chunk_findings.detail:
The close test `elif not line.strip().strip("`~")` is true for a blank code line, and blank lines inside a fence are yielded with `code=True` (they must be — the same branch is what recognises the opening fence line at line 119). So `fence` is reset to `None` in the middle of a block. For

```
# API
```python
x = 1

y = 2
```
```

the blank line clears `fence`; the next line `y = 2` then hits the `fence is None` branch, `_FENCE_OPEN.match("y = 2")` returns `None`, so `fence` becomes `""` and line 123 appends that `""` to `code_langs` for every live part. Result: `code_langs == ["python", ""]` for one python block, violating `Part`'s documented "one entry per fenced block" (line 40) and skewing any `code_blocks` check that names no lang (counts entries) or matches lang `""` — e.g. a one-block document satisfies a `min = 2` untagged-block rule. The same test also closes a ```` ``` ```` block on a content line consisting only of tildes (`~~~`), because it strips both fence characters and never compares against the opener's character or length.

chunk_findings.detail:
Table detection is `_DELIM.match(line) and _ROW.match(prev)`, where `_DELIM` deliberately makes the outer pipes optional (`\|?`) but `_ROW` requires both a leading and a trailing `|`. A GFM-style table without outer pipes is therefore never counted:

```
a | b
--- | ---
1 | 2
```

`_DELIM` matches `--- | ---` and the delimiter row is the current line, but `_ROW.match("a | b")` fails, so `tables == 0`. Any shipped `has_table` per-section rule rejects this valid table; the asymmetry with `_DELIM` shows the pipe-less form was intended to be supported.

chunk_findings.detail: `_row_at` deliberately handles the "nothing found" case by returning `max(len(rows) - 1, 0)`, which is `0` for an empty `rows`. Its only caller, `forbidden_whole_text`, then indexes the list directly: `line = rows[_row_at(rows, m.start())][0]`. When the scope's prose is empty (`ctx.prose(r) == []`) — e.g. a section that consists only of a heading plus a fenced code block, a missing/empty document, or a scope the helper resolves to no prose — and the rule's regex can match the empty string (`rx.search("\n".join([]))` matches on `""`), `m` is a truthy match object, `_row_at([], 0)` returns `0`, and `rows[0]` raises `IndexError`. Concretely, a type declaring `kind = "forbidden_whole_text"` with `regex = "\s*"` (a regex whose intent is "this section must not be blank") run against such a section aborts `ddflow docs check` with an unhandled exception instead of emitting a finding, taking down the whole run/digest for that document. The guard should be in the caller (skip when `rows` is empty or use the returned line number only when `rows` is non-empty).

chunk_findings.detail: `_TYPES.get(name, object)` falls back to the builtin `object` for any type name that is not in the four-entry table, and `isinstance(v, object)` is always true. So a schema that uses a valid JSON-Schema type the subset does not model — notably `"object"` and `"null"` — or that simply contains a typo (`"strin"`, `"integre"`) silently validates *everything* and never reports a problem. Concrete case: schema `{"properties": {"meta": {"type": "object"}}}`, front matter `{"meta": "just a string"}` — `schema_problems` yields nothing, so `front_matter` produces no finding even though the property has the wrong type; likewise `{"type": "null"}` accepts any non-null value. A misspelled `type` in a type's TOML therefore disables that property's check entirely instead of being flagged as an unsupported type, letting non-conforming front matter through `ddflow docs check`.

chunk_findings.detail: The `try/except re.error` in `_locate` is placed around the *construction* of the matcher lambda, not around its *use*, so the `except` clause is unreachable: for `match == "regex"` the lambda body `re.fullmatch(heading, t)` is only executed later, in the comprehension `hits = [p for p in self.doc.parts if ok(p.heading.text)]` at line 57. Given a type descriptor whose section heading is an invalid regular expression (e.g. `heading = "Overview("` with `match = "regex"` in the type TOML), `re.fullmatch` raises `re.error` at line 57, which propagates out of `Ctx.__post_init__` and out of `validate()` instead of being turned into a finding. chunk_findings.detail:
`_ROW` was widened from `^\s*\|.*\|\s*$` (leading *and* trailing outer pipe required) to `^.*\|.*$` (any line containing a pipe). Its sibling `_DELIM` regex is deliberately permissive and accepts a bare `---` (or `----`) as a valid one-column delimiter row: `^\s*\|?\s*:?-{2,}:?...` matches `---` with every optional group empty. Table detection is `_DELIM.match(line) and _ROW.match(prev)`, so any line containing a pipe that is immediately followed by `---` now counts as a table. Concrete input:

```
The two flags are `--a | --b`
---
```

Markdown renders this as a setext heading (or, after a list item, a thematic break), not a table, but `_DELIM.match("---")` is true and `_ROW.match("The two flags are `--a | --b`")` is now also true, so `tables` becomes 1 for that section. Before this change the same input yielded `tables == 0` because `_ROW` required outer pipes, so this is a new false positive: a section rule of the `has_table` family (e.g. a required table) is satisfied by prose that merely contains a `|` above a `---` rule, and the structural parse can no longer be trusted for those sections. The same happens with any `prev` line containing a single pipe above a one-cell delimiter such as `--- | ---`, since the parser does not compare cell counts.

chunk_findings.detail:
`re.compile(..., re.I)` makes the `match == "regex"` branch case-insensitive, whereas `re.fullmatch(heading, t)` in the previous code used the default flags and was case-sensitive. Rules are TOML data, so this loosens every existing regex heading check in any type descriptor without the type changing. Concrete case: a type with `[[sections]] heading = "^API$"`, `match = "regex"` (author intent: the section must be titled `API`) — previously a document containing `## api` failed the required-section/order check, now `_locate` returns that part and the check passes. Symmetrically, `heading = "^[A-Z][a-z]+$"` now accepts `## overview`. None of the new tests cover this (the added heading test only exercises `spec`'s load-time refusal of an invalid regex), so the semantic change is untested and undocumented; if case-insensitive regex matching is intended it should be an explicit, tested decision rather than a side effect of fixing the unreachable `except`. To preserve the old behaviour the regex branch must be compiled without `re.I`:

```python
rx = re.compile(heading if match == "regex" else re.escape(heading),
                0 if match == "regex" else re.I)
```

(The previously reported `_locate` defect — the `try/except re.error` wrapping the lambda *construction* instead of its *use* — is indeed fixed by this delta: the compile now happens inside the `try`, and a hand-built type with `heading = "Over("` reads as absent rather than raising. Confirmed findings 2, 4, 5, 6 each have a matching regression test here; finding 1 is refuted and finding 3 was superseded, so none are re-reported.)

chunk_findings.detail: `report.checked["doctypes"] = count` stores a bare `int` in the same mapping that other check families populate with collections: the surrounding, unchanged code in `docscheck_run.py:143` does `docs = set(report.checked["docs"])` to build the set of checked documents passed to `restrict()`. That line can only work because `checked` values are iterables (paths/kinds), so storing an `int` here breaks the invariant of the mapping. Any consumer that treats `checked` uniformly — iterating a family's value, calling `len(v)` to render the per-family count in the digest, or wrapping it with `set()` the way the diff path already wraps `"docs"` — will raise `TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable` / `object of type 'int' has no len()` as soon as a document is validated, which happens on every run because shipped types are always loaded via `types_of()`. chunk_findings.detail:
The closing-fence test `elif not line.strip().strip("`~")` is true for *any* line that is whitespace-only, not just a real fence line, because `"".strip()` is already `""`. Blank lines inside a fenced block are common, and they are yielded by `lines()` with `code=True`, so they reach this branch with `fence` set. Given

```
## S
```python
a = 1

b = 2
```
```

the first code line sets `fence="python"` and appends `"python"` to every live part; the empty line then clears `fence`; the next code line (`b = 2`) has `code=True` and `fence is None`, so it is taken as a *new* opening fence, `_FENCE_OPEN` does not match it, and `""` is appended as a code language. `Part.code_langs` therefore becomes `["python", ""]` instead of `["python"]`. With two or more blank lines a single block is reported as three or more blocks. Any rule that counts blocks (`code_blocks {lang, min}`) or flags untagged fences then sees a number that does not correspond to the document — the inflated count can satisfy a `min` for a section that really contains only one block, and spurious `""` entries can trip an "every block declares a language" style check. The close should be tested against the opening fence character and its length, and should not treat an empty line as a close.

chunk_findings.detail: `prev` is initialized to `0` (line 52), which is the document-root level the markdownlint/MD001-style check is supposed to compare the first heading against, but the condition is guarded with `if prev and ...`. Because `0` is falsy, the first heading of the document is never checked: given a document whose first heading is `### Deep` (or `## Overview`) and no preceding heading, `no_skipped_levels` yields no finding at all, even though the level jumps from the root 0 to 2/3. The reference markdownlint MD001 compares against `prevLevel = 0` without a truthiness guard and does report "Expected: h1; Actual: h2" for such input, so this silently drops a whole class of skipped-level documents (any doc that starts below H1 with no heading before it; here the `prev = 0` initialization is dead). The concrete failing input is a single `## Overview` heading at line 1 — the loop enters with `prev == 0`, the `and` short-circuits, and no finding is emitted.

The fix is to compile/validate the pattern before the comprehension (or wrap the comprehension itself), returning a finding/None as the `except` intends.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_ROW` was changed from `^\s*\|.*\|\s*$` (a row must have an outer pipe) to `^.*\|.*$` (any line containing a pipe anywhere). Because `_read` accepts a table when the current line matches `_DELIM` and the *previous* line matches `_ROW`, and `_DELIM` (`^\s*\|?\s*:?-{2,}:?\s*(\|\s*:?-{2,}:?\s*)*\|?\s*$`) deliberately makes the outer pipes optional so that a bare `---` is a valid one-cell delimiter row, the broadened `_ROW` now turns an ordinary prose line containing a pipe that is followed by a setext underline / rule into a table. Input: ``` Options a | b --- ``` `_ROW.match("Options a | b")` succeeds (previously it failed: no leading pipe), and `_DELIM.match("---")` succeeds, so `table` becomes `True` in `_read`, whereas GFM parses this pair as a setext heading (`

Options a | b

` — the header row has 2 cells, the delimiter row 1, so it is not a table). Any doctype with `has_table: true` (or any rule keyed on `Part.tables`) therefore reports the requirement as met for a document that contains no table, i.e. the validation silently passes a document it should reject. The same trigger occurs after a list item or paragraph that merely mentions a pipe, e.g. `- run `a | b`` followed by `---`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The refactor compiles the heading pattern with `re.I` for *both* branches:

```python
rx = re.compile(heading if match == "regex" else re.escape(heading), re.I)
hits = [p for p in self.doc.parts if rx.fullmatch(p.heading.text)]
```

Before this change the two cases were deliberately different: the literal branch used `t.casefold() == heading.casefold()` (case-insensitive), while the regex branch used a bare `re.fullmatch(heading, t)` with **no flags** (case-sensitive). Folding both onto one compile silently turns every `match = "regex"` heading into a case-insensitive match, which is not what the old code did.

Concrete failure: a type with `[[doctype.sections]] id = "risk" heading = "^Risks$" match = "regex" level = 2` previously located only `## Risks`. Now `_locate` also matches `## risks` / `## RISKS` and, since the fallback is `hits[0]`, can bind the section (and all of its per-section rules: `required_text`, `forbidden_text`, word bounds, `has_table`, …) to a heading the regex was written to exclude. The regex author's intent is lost: any pattern relying on case to discriminate (e.g. an anchor like `^[A-Z]` to require an upper-case heading, or two sibling sections whose patterns differ only in case) now matches unintended parts, which can both hide a missing required section and apply content rules to the wrong section. `hits[0]` fallback makes the wrong-part selection non-deterministic in ordering, so the failure is input-order dependent. The new tests only cover load-time rejection of a bad regex (`test_a_heading_regex_that_does_not_compile_is_refused_at_load`), so nothing pins the regex branch's case sensitivity.

This directly contradicts the module's stated contract in the same file (line 6-7: "A rule that cannot be applied (a bad regex, a link target it cannot read) is a finding saying so, never silence") and the change's intent that heading regexes are a supported rule input. chunk_findings.detail:
`_ROW` was changed from `^\s*\|.*\|\s*$` (a row must have an outer pipe) to `^.*\|.*$` (any line containing a pipe anywhere). Because `_read` accepts a table when the current line matches `_DELIM` and the *previous* line matches `_ROW`, and `_DELIM` (`^\s*\|?\s*:?-{2,}:?\s*(\|\s*:?-{2,}:?\s*)*\|?\s*$`) deliberately makes the outer pipes optional so that a bare `---` is a valid one-cell delimiter row, the broadened `_ROW` now turns an ordinary prose line containing a pipe that is followed by a setext underline / rule into a table. Input: ``` Options a | b --- ``` `_ROW.match("Options a | b")` succeeds (previously it failed: no leading pipe), and `_DELIM.match("---")` succeeds, so `table` becomes `True` in `_read`, whereas GFM parses this pair as a setext heading (`

Options a | b

` — the header row has 2 cells, the delimiter row 1, so it is not a table). Any doctype with `has_table: true` (or any rule keyed on `Part.tables`) therefore reports the requirement as met for a document that contains no table, i.e. the validation silently passes a document it should reject. The same trigger occurs after a list item or paragraph that merely mentions a pipe, e.g. `- run `a | b`` followed by `---`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The refactor compiles the heading pattern with `re.I` for *both* branches:

```python
rx = re.compile(heading if match == "regex" else re.escape(heading), re.I)
hits = [p for p in self.doc.parts if rx.fullmatch(p.heading.text)]
```

Before this change the two cases were deliberately different: the literal branch used `t.casefold() == heading.casefold()` (case-insensitive), while the regex branch used a bare `re.fullmatch(heading, t)` with **no flags** (case-sensitive). Folding both onto one compile silently turns every `match = "regex"` heading into a case-insensitive match, which is not what the old code did.

Concrete failure: a type with `[[doctype.sections]] id = "risk" heading = "^Risks$" match = "regex" level = 2` previously located only `## Risks`. Now `_locate` also matches `## risks` / `## RISKS` and, since the fallback is `hits[0]`, can bind the section (and all of its per-section rules: `required_text`, `forbidden_text`, word bounds, `has_table`, …) to a heading the regex was written to exclude. The regex author's intent is lost: any pattern relying on case to discriminate (e.g. an anchor like `^[A-Z]` to require an upper-case heading, or two sibling sections whose patterns differ only in case) now matches unintended parts, which can both hide a missing required section and apply content rules to the wrong section. `hits[0]` fallback makes the wrong-part selection non-deterministic in ordering, so the failure is input-order dependent. The new tests only cover load-time rejection of a bad regex (`test_a_heading_regex_that_does_not_compile_is_refused_at_load`), so nothing pins the regex branch's case sensitivity.

chunk_findings.detail: The rule is registered with `--globs "docs/**/*.md"`, but the item that is supposed to pick it up is created with `--globs "docs/a.md"` — a file sitting directly under `docs/`. The behaviour this change documents is "a rule on `docs/**.md` reaches the brief of an item touching `docs/a.md`" — i.e. a pattern whose wildcard spans the path separator, the way `fnmatch`-style rule matching works (`docs/**.md` compiles to `docs/.*.*\.md`, which matches `docs/a.md`). The pattern actually written in the test requires a second `/`-separated segment between `docs/` and the filename, so `docs/a.md` does not match it and no overlap with the item's globs is found. Concretely: given rule glob `docs/**/*.md` and item globs `docs/a.md`, `run_cli(repo, "brief", "--item", "DOCS")` returns guidance without `id="r-prose"`, so the assertion on line 109 fails (and likewise the claim assertion on line 111); only the negative assertion for `SRC` on line 110 passes, so the test as written never demonstrates the behaviour it is named after. Either the pattern must be the documented `docs/**.md` (or `docs/**`), or the item must be a nested path such as `docs/sub/a.md` for the assertion to be about the intended rule-to-document wiring.
